paragraphs: Shimon ha-Temani. In Mishnah Ta'anit, chapter 3, 19a, Rashi explains that he was from Timnah, as it is written, “Shimshon, the Timnite's son-in-law,” after Timnat. Sefer Lehem Shamayim writes that this is because his reading was ha-Timni, the tav with a hiriq, as in “Shimshon, the Timnite's son-in-law.” We read ha-Temani, the tav with a tzere and the mem with a kamatz, as the Torah writes, “Husham from the land of the Temanite.” It is not strange to say that he was from the land of Teman, outside the Land of Israel, as we find with several tannaim, whereas the aforementioned town is in the Land of Israel. In Yadayim 1:3; the Mishnah at the end of Yevamot, chapter 4, 49a, with R' Akiva; Ha-Hovel, 90b; and Yom Tov, 21a, where he did not come on the festival night to the study hall, and in the morning R' Yehudah ben Bava found him, and so forth. Thus he was their colleague, but he calls R' Akiva “my teacher,” saying, “I hereby add to my teacher's words”: Sifrei. He is one of the four sages of Yavneh—R' Eliezer, R' Yehoshua, R' Akiva, and he—arguing before them while seated on the ground. He is one of the five who argued before the sages; see Danin. And R' Shimon ben Menasya: Ketubbot 29b; there, 36 beginning of side a, Tosafot בשס״ח [provisionally in the new Talmud editions; uncollated] say that he was his disputant. Shimon ha-Temani asked Rabban Gamliel; see his entry. This is puzzling unless we say that there were two. Rambam writes that he is mentioned only in Yevamot, chapter 4; from the foregoing, he is mentioned more often.
